title: US considers diesel export restrictions | Wood Mackenzie
gist: With US diesel prices near record highs ahead of the 3 November midterms, the Trump administration is weighing diesel export restrictions; Wood Mackenzie's refinery modelling says a ban would cut Gulf Coast crude runs, lower gasoline output and raise US East Coast gasoline prices ~15% (~26c/gal) while lifting NW Europe diesel ~27%, so 'voluntary' industry curbs or earmarked cheap supply are the likelier outcome. Briefs cover repeated Iran/Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's Yanbu/East-West pipeline bypass route, Fervo's first utility-scale enhanced geothermal power, stalled permitting reform, and off-grid solar growth in Sub-Saharan Africa.

insights.claim: US diesel prices are at or near record highs, severe enough that Louisiana declared a state of emergency allowing farmers and loggers to use lower-taxed dyed diesel in on-road vehicles for a month.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Distillate tightness is acute enough to trigger state-level emergency measures even in oil-producing states; signals strong political pressure on refiners and diesel cracks.
insights.quote: The fact that even Louisiana, a heartland of the US oil and gas industry, has been forced to take action to cushion the blow from fuel costs is a sign of the severity of the crisis.
insights.locator: Louisiana’s Governor Jeff Landry this week

insights.claim: The Trump administration is split on a US diesel export ban: President Trump and Senator Chuck Grassley back it, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the API and AFPM oppose it, and a reported 90-day ban was quickly denied.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Policy headline risk for US refiners and product cracks remains elevated until a formal decision; watch White House announcements.
insights.quote: The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn't work.
insights.locator: Chris Wright, the energy secretary, said

insights.claim: A negotiated arrangement with refiners, such as 'voluntary' export curbs or earmarking a share of output for lower-priced sales to farmers, is more likely than an outright US diesel export ban.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Expect a softer intervention that dents refiner margins modestly rather than a full export shutdown; position for margin drag, not a Gulf Coast run collapse.
insights.quote: But some agreement with the industry along those lines seems more likely than an outright export ban.

insights.claim: An earmarked cheap-diesel scheme for farmers would face significant administrative hurdles, including deciding which refiners contribute and who qualifies for the fuel.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Implementation friction could delay or dilute any voluntary scheme, prolonging uncertainty for refiners.

insights.claim: With retail diesel near record levels and the 3 November midterms approaching, pressure on the administration to intervene in diesel markets will keep growing, and any intervention that overrides market mechanisms would make US refining less efficient.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Some form of government action on diesel before the midterms is likely; treat US refiners as carrying pre-election policy risk.
insights.quote: the pressure on the administration to do something is only going to grow.

themes.theme: Why a ban backfires on US consumers

insights.claim: US diesel and gasoil exports ran at about 1 million b/d over the summer; under a ban refiners could only partly cut diesel yields, would fill storage, and then be forced to cut crude runs.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: An export ban is effectively a forced run cut for export-oriented refiners, hitting throughput and co-product output.
insights.locator: The reasons lie in the dynamics

insights.claim: The impact of a US diesel export ban would be concentrated on the Gulf Coast, which holds the bulk of US crude distillation capacity and virtually all deepwater export infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Gulf Coast-heavy refiners are most exposed to export restrictions; inland/mid-continent refiners less so.
insights.quote: If exports were cut off, it would be Gulf Coast barrels that would have nowhere to go.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Refinery Supply Model estimates a US diesel export ban would cut diesel/gasoil production by about 800,000 b/d and gasoline production by about 70,000 b/d.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Quantifies the co-product hit: a diesel policy would tighten US gasoline supply.
insights.locator: The result would be that US gasoline production would fall

insights.claim: A US diesel export ban would raise US East Coast gasoline prices by about 15% versus Wood Mackenzie's base case, roughly 26 cents a gallon, pushing gasoline towards record highs.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: A ban would be bullish for East Coast gasoline cracks and RBOB; politically self-defeating ahead of the midterms.
insights.quote: A policy designed to bring relief at the diesel pump could end up driving prices higher at the gasoline pump.
insights.locator: We estimate that would raise gasoline prices

insights.claim: A US diesel export ban would lower diesel prices in most of the US but raise them in the import-reliant North-East, since the East Coast imported about 120,000 b/d of diesel last year and is tied to international prices.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Regional price divergence: Gulf/inland diesel falls while New York Harbor-linked diesel could rise.
insights.locator: Another direct effect on the US

insights.claim: Fuel export bans have precedents: Russia banned diesel exports in July after Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries, and China curbed oil product exports in March and still runs an export quota system.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Global product supply is already constrained by other exporters' curbs, amplifying the impact of any US restriction.
insights.locator: The appeal of banning fuel exports

insights.claim: A US diesel export ban would lift North-West Europe diesel prices about 27% above Wood Mackenzie's base case, roughly 80 cents per gallon, prompting President Macron to urge Trump not to impose one.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: European refiners would be big winners and European diesel consumers big losers; ICE gasoil is the key tail-risk instrument.
insights.locator: US diesel prices would indeed fall

insights.claim: Higher fuel costs in Europe and Mexico from a US diesel export ban would feed through into higher prices for goods they sell to the US, adding to US inflation.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Second-round inflation effects would complicate the Fed's response to already high oil prices.
insights.locator: There would also be second-round effects

themes.theme: Saudi Red Sea export route under attack

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Yanbu port, the main bypass of the Strait of Hormuz, have been attacked repeatedly by Iran and the Houthis since the conflict began in late February; France has pledged soldiers, radars and defence systems to protect Yanbu.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Saudi export redundancy around Hormuz is compromised, sustaining a geopolitical risk premium in crude.
insights.locator: France has promised to send troops

insights.claim: The East-West pipeline restarted after an 11-day shutdown from drone strikes on the pipe and three pumping stations, and is expected to reach 40% of normal capacity within two days, but a full restart will take six to eight weeks and Yanbu tanker loadings have not resumed.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Saudi Red Sea export capacity stays impaired for weeks, keeping crude and product markets tight into late 2026.
insights.locator: Flows on the East-West pipeline restarted

insights.claim: Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah has produced first power, the first utility-scale enhanced geothermal project to generate electricity, with its 100 MW first phase due to start up fully by 1 January 2027 and a 400 MW second phase under construction for 2028.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Commercial proof point for enhanced geothermal using oil-and-gas horizontal drilling; relevant to firm clean power supply and oilfield services crossover.
insights.locator: The enhanced geothermal company Fervo Energy

insights.claim: Bipartisan US permitting reform for fossil and renewable infrastructure has stalled and will not pass before the 3 November midterms; Energy Secretary Wright hopes for passage in the lame-duck session.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Infrastructure developers face continued permitting delays; lame-duck session is the next catalyst.
insights.locator: Negotiations in the US Congress over reform

insights.claim: Off-grid solar capacity in Sub-Saharan Africa is growing rapidly on high diesel prices, low solar costs and better financing, and Wood Mackenzie expects growth to continue for at least ten years, with 600 million people still lacking reliable electricity.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: High diesel prices strengthen the economics of distributed solar displacing diesel generators in Africa, a multi-gigawatt market.

insights.claim: Demis Hassabis argues AI's impact could be 10x the Industrial Revolution at 10x the speed and calls for a new standards body or self-regulatory organisation for the AI industry to manage risks including nuclear and biological threats.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Signals industry-led push toward AI self-regulation; watch for standards-body formation affecting AI developers.
insights.quote: perhaps 10x of the Industrial Revolution at 10x the speed
